item.title: Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope
item.description: Dev Kapadia’s de:volt is a breadboard simulator that runs in your browser. You can place parts and wires on a breadboard, and the circuit runs live the whole time as you build it. The project aims to be as close as a real breadboard would be. It reports errors and warnings, and you can monitor pins with its built-in oscilloscope and/or multimeter. For instance, an LED with no resistor burns out, a weak battery sags under load, a motor pulls current, and a 555 on the 4-channel scope shows its timing capacitor charging and discharging. de:volt highlights: Build circuits on a virtual breadboard using the 105 parts available from the interface: resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, LEDs, 555 timers, 74-series and CD4000 logic, EEPROMs, motor drivers, sensors, and more. Four Arduino, BBC micro:bit, and RP2040 MCU boards are also available, and you can write and run MicroPython code from the web [...] The post Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope appeared first on CNX Software - Embedded Systems News.

item.title: 750 MHz GigaDevice GD32H7 Cortex-M7 MCU family gets up to 9.5MB Flash, EtherCAT for industrial applications
item.description: GigaDevice adds new industrial parts to the GD32H7 series of Cortex-M7 MCUs, running at up to 750 MHz. The new lineup includes the GD32H77R for robotic joint control, GD32H78D/77D for industrial HMI applications, GD32H78E/77E for real-time motion control, and GD32H789/779 for general industrial automation. The MCUs feature up to 9728KB of on-chip Flash, 1152KB SRAM including 640KB tightly coupled memory (TCM), and hardware accelerators for mathematical operations and digital signal processing. Depending on the variant, they also integrate a MIPI DSI display interface, an EtherCAT slave controller, industrial encoder interfaces, dual Ethernet, and three CAN-FD controllers. The devices target servo drives, humanoid robots, industrial displays, CNC machines, PLCs, and digital power systems. item.title: Renesas RZ/T2N Cortex-A55/R52 industrial MPU supports four-axis motor control, TSN Ethernet, EtherCAT…
item.description: Renesas RZ/T2N industrial MPU supports up to four-axis motor control and includes PWM timers, encoder interfaces, and trigonometric accelerators. It’s designed for industrial robots, programmable logic controllers (PLCs), motion controllers, and multi-axis servo drives. The MPU features up to two 1.2 GHz Arm Cortex-A55 cores for application processing and two 800 MHz Cortex-R52 cores for real-time control. It also integrates a three-port Gigabit Ethernet switch with TSN support and industrial Ethernet protocols such as EtherCAT, PROFINET RT/IRT, and EtherNet/IP. This feature set allows real-time motor control, industrial networking, and Linux applications to run on a single chip, reducing the need for separate processors. The MPU can also work as an industrial Ethernet network controller or device, depending on the application. item.title: LabWired allows engineers to test compiled firmware on simulated MCU boards (CPU and peripherals)
item.description: Andrii Shylenko’s LabWired is an MIT-licensed MCU firmware simulation core that runs compiled firmware against modeled CPUs and peripherals, captures UART and bus output, register state, and supports repeatable checks in CI. The simulator works on Arm Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M3, Cortex-M4, Cortex-M7, Cortex-M33 cores, RISC-V architecutre, and Xtensa LX6 and LX7 (some ESP32 parts). The main benefit of the project is speeding up firmware testing since doing some on real boards is slow. The hardware must be ready, then the firmware must be flashed to the board each time you want to test it, and if something breaks, developers get a dark LED and no trace. If a firmware project needs to support multiple boards, this quickly adds up. The project is different from a CPU/MCU emulator for two main reasons: The full board is modeled, not only the chip. Sensors, displays, and bus devices are also simulated. item.title: KiCad 10 now (unofficially) runs in a web browser or Android
item.description: It’s now possible to run KiCad 10 directly in a web browser or as an Android app thanks to two separate open-source projects, unaffiliated with the official KiCad project. Let’s have a look at both. Ziro Designer/ZiroEDA – KiCad 10 in your web browser Akshay Rukade (ZiroEDA), an engineering student in India, ported KiCad 10.0.6 to the browser through the Ziro Designer/ZiroEDA Designer project. It’s a TypeScript translation of KiCad’s C++, kept file-for-file against the KiCad implementation, so the real schematic editor, PCB editor, interactive router, and ERC/DRC run in a browser tab and read and write normal KiCad projects. That means you can open local KiCad projects or designs hosted on GitHub directly in a web browser without having to install KiCad 10 itself on your computer, and it should also enable machines that do not natively support KiCad (e.g., RISC-V, Android tablet, iPad…) to run it. item.description: DomeCtrl’s ControlBox is a Raspberry Pi 5-based controller running Home Assistant and primarily designed for hydronic radiant floor heating (RFH) systems. item.title: Seeed Studio XIAO STM32C5 development board features dual CAN FD and a 6-axis IMU with programmable heating
item.description: Seeed Studio XIAO STM32C5 is the company’s first XIAO development board based on an STMicroelectronics MCU, namely a 144 MHz STM32C5A3CG Arm Cortex-M33 microcontroller. It features two CAN FD controllers and a 6-axis IMU with programmable heating for robotics, industrial control, and motion-sensing applications. The board also includes 16MB of external flash, a 48 MHz external crystal, a USB-C port, and battery charging circuitry. The integrated IMU heater allows firmware to control sensor temperature and reduce measurement drift from temperature changes. item.title: Waveshare ESP32-S31-Zero – A tiny ESP32-S31 board with up to 32MB PSRAM, 32MB SPI flash
item.description: Waveshare ESP32-S31-Zero is a small ESP32-S31 development board that follows the form factor of the earlier Waveshare “Zero” boards, such as the ESP32-C6-Zero-B, RA4M1-Zero, and ESP32-S3-Zero, among others. The new tiny board still features a USB-C port for power and programming, as well as eighteen through and castellated holes for GPIO and power signals, but it boasts a more powerful ESP32-S31 dual-core RISC-V MCU clocked at up to 320 MHz, featuring 2.4 GHz WiFi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, and 802.15.4 connectivity, as well as up to 32MB on-chip PSRAM and a 16MB or 32MB SPI flash chip. item.title: 520 MHz STM32H7P4/STM32H7P5 Arm Cortex-M7 MCUs feature Hardware Signal Processor (HSP), optional Neural-ART NPU
item.description: STMicroelectronics has introduced the STM32H7P4 and STM32H7P5, two 520 MHz Arm Cortex-M7 MCUs part of STM32H7P family designed for digital power, motor control, industrial sensing, and edge AI applications. Both feature a Hardware Signal Processor (HSP) for accelerating mathematical and signal-processing operations, while the STM32H7P5 also includes an 85 GOPS Neural-ART NPU for Edge AI inference/TinyML.
